statement:
(i) In the differential equation
$$\frac{1}{y^2}\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{y}=e^{2x},$$
make the substitution $u=1/y$, and hence show that the general solution of the original equation is
$$y=\frac{1}{Ae^x-e^{2x}}.$$

(ii) Use a similar method to solve the equation
$$\frac{1}{y^3}\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{y^2}=e^{2x}.$$
solution:
(i) Let $u=1/y$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx}=-\dfrac{1}{y^2}\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. Substituting into the equation,
$$-\frac{du}{dx}+u=e^{2x} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{du}{dx}-u=-e^{2x}.$$

This is linear in $u$ with integrating factor $e^{-x}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(ue^{-x}\right)=-e^{x}.$$
Integrating, $ue^{-x}=-e^{x}+A$, so $u=Ae^{x}-e^{2x}$. Therefore
$$y=\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{Ae^x-e^{2x}}.$$

(ii) Let $u=1/y^2$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx}=-\dfrac{2}{y^3}\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. Substituting,
$$-\frac12\frac{du}{dx}+u=e^{2x} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{du}{dx}-2u=-2e^{2x}.$$

This is linear with integrating factor $e^{-2x}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(ue^{-2x}\right)=-2.$$
Integrating, $ue^{-2x}=-2x+A$, so $u=(A-2x)e^{2x}$. Therefore
$$\frac{1}{y^2}=(A-2x)e^{2x} \quad\Rightarrow\quad y^2=\frac{e^{-2x}}{A-2x},$$
and hence
$$y=\pm\frac{e^{-x}}{\sqrt{A-2x}}.$$
hints: Substitute u=1/y (or u=1/y²) and note how du/dx relates to the dy/dx term.
The equation becomes linear in u, solvable with an integrating factor.
Solve for u then convert back to y.
